19.0.big: Evolution happens to populations, not individuals. This chapter is about how and why a population's genes change from one generation to the next.
points: Example: the Florida panther nearly died out from too little genetic variety until panthers from Texas were brought in.

19.1.big: Population genetics joins Mendel (how genes are inherited) with Darwin (natural selection). That combo is called the modern synthesis.
points: Microevolution = changes in allele frequencies in a population over generations. Macroevolution = bigger changes over long times, like new species.
The gene pool is every allele in the population. Genetic structure = its allele and genotype frequencies.
Hardy–Weinberg principle of equilibrium: allele frequencies stay the same unless something changes them.
The five conditions for no evolution: no mutation, no migration (gene flow), a very large population (no drift), random mating, and no natural selection. Break any one and the population evolves.
The math: p + q = 1 (allele frequencies) and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (genotype frequencies: AA, Aa, aa).
Trick: count the recessive-looking individuals first. That number is q². Take the square root to get q, then p = 1 − q.
19.1.tip: Example: 16% of flowers are white (recessive). q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4, p = 0.6. Heterozygotes = 2pq = 0.48.

19.2.big: Five forces change a population's genes: natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow, mutation, and nonrandom mating.
points: Population variation is the spread of phenotypes. Only the part caused by genes (heritability) can evolve. Different alleles of the same gene are polymorphisms.
Genetic drift = allele frequencies change by chance. It's strongest in small populations.
Bottleneck effect: a disaster wipes out most of a population at random, so the survivors' genes take over. Founder effect: a small group starts a new population, carrying only some of the alleles.
Gene flow = alleles move between populations as individuals or pollen migrate. It makes populations more alike.
Mutation is the only source of brand-new alleles. Most mutations are harmful or neutral.
Nonrandom mating: assortative mating (picking mates like yourself) and inbreeding. Inbreeding exposes rare harmful recessive alleles, which is called inbreeding depression.
Environment can change phenotypes too. Geographical variation across a gradual environmental change (like warmer to colder) is a cline.
Fitness = how many offspring you leave. Relative fitness compares that to others in the population.
19.2.tip: Bottleneck = population shrinks in place. Founder = a few move away and start over.

19.3.big: Natural selection can push a trait in different directions. Draw the bell curve before and after to see which type it is.
points: Stabilizing selection: the middle is favored and the extremes lose (like average-weight human babies). The curve gets narrower.
Directional selection: one extreme is favored (dark peppered moths during pollution). The curve shifts to one side.
Diversifying selection: both extremes win and the middle loses. The curve splits into two peaks, and variation goes up.
Frequency-dependent selection: a phenotype's fitness depends on how common it is. Negative = rare types win (side-blotched lizards). Positive = common types win.

Sexual selection leads to sexual dimorphism (males and females look different, like peacocks). The handicap principle says a costly ornament is an honest signal of good health. The good genes hypothesis says females pick males with ornaments because they carry good genes.
There's no perfect organism: selection can only work with the variation that already exists, and traits trade off against each other.
Selection that improves the fit between a population and its environment is adaptive evolution, driven by a selective pressure.
19.3.tip: Stabilizing squeezes the middle. Directional slides it over. Diversifying splits it in two.

2.why: Males leave and join other groups, carrying their alleles with them: gene flow.

4.why: Micro = allele changes within populations. Macro = changes in species over long times.

5.why: Lamarck thought traits earned during life (strong arms from use) get passed to offspring. That's wrong, but it's his idea.

6.why: Genes, environment and diet all shape the phenotypes you see.

7.why: Genetic variance = the diversity of alleles and genotypes in a population.

8.why: Relatives share the same rare harmful recessive alleles, so inbred offspring are more likely to get two copies.

9.why: A natural disaster kills randomly, which is genetic drift (a bottleneck).

12.why: A cline is a gradual change across a range, like more cold tolerance in colder areas.

13.why: Diversifying favors both extremes, so variation goes up.

15.why: It explains showy ornaments: they advertise good genes to mates.

16.why: Males and females looking different = sexual dimorphism.

17.why: Natural selection = better-adapted organisms survive and reproduce more, like finch beaks changing with seed size.

19.why: New alleles come from mutation or gene flow, and they become common only if selection favors them.

20.why: Population variation = the spread of phenotypes, like all the fur colors in dogs.

21.why: A few individuals leave and start a new population with only some of the colors: founder effect.

22.why: Founders come from the nearest island (H), so the new population should look like H's.

23.why: A cline is variation that changes gradually across a gradient, like bigger bodies toward the poles.

24.why: Probably yes. It's a small population, and the brown and black numbers bounce up and down with no steady trend. Random ups and downs in a small population are the sign of drift, not selection.

25.why: The big alpha male and the small sneaky males both mate, while the medium males lose. Both extremes winning = diversifying selection.

26.why: Selection can only work with the variation that already exists.

27.why: The curve should shift toward smaller body sizes in the new population, because small mice escape the predator. That's directional selection.

28.why: The drug's effectiveness drops over time as resistant parasites survive and multiply. That's directional selection toward drug resistance.

29.why: A falls steadily (0.80 to 0.39) while B rises. A steady trend, not random wobbling, means selection against A.

30.why: Pop 1: A rises steadily, so selection favors A. Pop 2: A appears out of nowhere (from deer in the nearby forest), so that's gene flow, and then A keeps rising.

31.why: Grass that flowers before the mower comes gets to reproduce, so the mowed field evolves to flower earlier.

32.why: Two peaks became one peak in the middle, so mid-sized mouthparts are favored: stabilizing natural selection.

33.why: p = q = 0.5, so we'd expect AA = p² = 25%. Seeing 35% is higher than expected, so evolution happened (aa fish likely died of disease).

34.why: Favoring heterozygotes means 2pq goes up, so the population is no longer in equilibrium.

35.why: With no migration, look at the graph's shape. A steady rise or fall in one allele means natural selection (selected for or against). Random ups and downs mean genetic drift, where the alleles are neutral.

36.why: With no migration and genes that don't affect each other, a steady trend in an allele means natural selection. Random wobbling means genetic drift. If neither changes, the population isn't evolving at that gene.

37.why: p = 0.7, q = 0.3. With random mating you'd get AA = 0.49, Aa = 0.42, aa = 0.09, so AA and aa each drop by 0.21, the same amount.

38.why: Wind now carries pollen (with allele C) from population 1 to the others. That's gene flow, which brings in C and lowers A and B in population 3.

39.why: Once the river dried up, blue and yellow individuals crossed over: more gene flow.

40.why: Each later year's curve sits farther right, so the fungus tolerates more fungicide: resistance from directional selection.
